```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  class.output = "r"
)
library(tidytargets)
library(dplyr)

work <- tempfile("tidytargets-vignette-")
dir.create(work)
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = work)
```

tidytargets is a tidy, pipe-friendly grammar for `{targets}`. 

`tt_initialise()` constructs a `tidytargets` object. Each method is a [target factory](https://books.ropensci.org/targets/static.html#target-factories): it records a `tar_target` definition on that object. You compose the pipeline with `|>`; `{targets}` runs the dependency graph.

The composition is **lazy**. `tt_initialise()`, `tt_data()`, `tt_data_list()`, `tt_global()`, `tt_single()`, `tt_iterate()`, `tt_split()`, `tt_merge()`, and `tt_report()` only add steps to the object. `{store}.R` is written from it by `tt_evaluate()` (or by `show_targets_script()`), which then runs `targets::tar_make()`; user functions are not called before that. Because the script is generated rather than accumulated, it always matches the object: declare a target name or a global twice and the second definition simply replaces the first.
Assigning the object does not print it, so an interactive session then says the pipeline is ready to be evaluated, rather than appearing to do nothing.

Pipelines are **incremental**. Add a step, change a parameter, or grow the input list and `{targets}` skips up-to-date targets, re-running only what the new graph requires. That is why this vignette can show the script after each building block without executing the pipeline.

This vignette walks through every building block and prints the targets script after each step with `show_targets_script()`.

## Building blocks

### Workflow

| Function | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `tt_initialise()` | Start a pipeline: configuration, optional mapped inputs |
| `tt_evaluate()` | Write the script and run `tar_make()` |
| `tt_script()` | Write the script without running it, so `tar_manifest()`, `tar_outdated()`, and `tar_visnetwork()` can inspect the graph |
| `tt_read()` | Read the full stored value of a named target |

### Data

| Function | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `tt_data()` | Snapshot a session object onto the store as one target |
| `tt_data_list()` | Snapshot a list onto the store as mapped units |
| `tt_global()` | Declare helper functions every target can call |
| `tt_merge()` | Combine iterated results into one object |
| `tt_split()` | Turn a pipeline list into mapped units |

### Commands

| Function | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `tt_iterate()` | Map a function over inputs |
| `tt_single()` | Add one non-iterated target |

`tt_factory()` is internal and used by the command functions above. `tt_single()`, `tt_iterate()`, `tt_split()`, and `tt_merge()` all append `target_list <- target_list |> target_append(tt_factory(...))` to the script.

### Reporting and debug

| Function | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `tt_report()` | Render a Quarto / R Markdown report |
| `tt_explore()` | Return one stored instance of a named target |
| `tt_metadata()` | Get or set free-form metadata on the pipeline object |

## Toy inputs

`tt_initialise()` can be called with no inputs (configuration and store only). A named list of in-memory objects, one element per unit of iteration (e.g. sample), registers mapped targets. `tt_data()` adds a session object later without splitting it; `tt_data_list()` adds a list as mapped units.

```{r inputs}
inputs <- list(
  sample_a = 1:3,
  sample_b = 4:6
)
```

## `tt_initialise()`

This writes `{store}.R` and saves configuration. If you passed mapped inputs, it also registers:

- `input_list` — the named input vector or list (override with `target_output`)
- `sample_names` — the names of that vector or list

With no `computing_resources`, the pipeline is sequential. With no `store`, a unique `./tidytargets-<HASH>` directory is created. With no inputs, start from `tt_initialise()` and add objects with `tt_data()`. By default `error = "continue"` so a failed target does not halt the rest of the pipeline; pass `error = "stop"` to halt on the first failure.

Packages currently attached in your session (`.packages()`) are recorded at `tt_initialise()` as names on `tar_option_set(packages = )` so workers can `library()` them. `tt_initialise()` messages that list so you can check the same packages are available on HPC. Objects in the global environment are not copied; bring those in with `tt_data()` or `user_function_source_path`. Pass `packages` to override the snapshot. Attach libraries before initialise (or pass `packages`) if a later command needs them.

```{r initialise}
pipe <- inputs |>
  tt_initialise()
```

```{r initialise-script, comment = ""}
show_targets_script(pipe)
```

## `tt_data()`

Write a local object onto the store as a single target. Unlike `tt_initialise()`, the value is not split into iteration units.

```{r data}
extra <- list(label = "demo")
pipe <- pipe |>
  tt_data(extra)
```

```{r data-script, comment = ""}
show_targets_script(pipe)
```

## `tt_data_list()`

Same snapshot, but each list element is a mapped unit. Use this for a parameter grid split into rows (`group_split(row_number())`). Name an inline expression with `<-`, or pass `target_output`.

```{r data-list}
grid <- expand.grid(alpha = c(0, 1), lambda = c(0.1, 1))
pipe <- pipe |>
  tt_data_list(settings <- grid |> group_split(row_number()))
```

```{r data-list-script, comment = ""}
show_targets_script(pipe)
```

## `tt_global()`

Helper functions are not data, so they do not belong in `tt_data()`. `tt_global()` records them on the pipeline object, and the generated script assigns them above the target list, where every target can call them. One global function can call another, so a helper never has to be passed as an argument just to reach the worker.

A global is not a target: it is not a node in the graph, is not stored in the object store, and is not read by `tt_read()`. `{targets}` still tracks which commands use it, so editing one invalidates the targets that call it and leaves the rest up to date.

```{r global}
scale_values <- function(x) x / max(x)
report_scale <- function(x) round(scale_values(x), 2)

pipe <- pipe |>
  tt_global(scale_values, report_scale)
```

```{r global-script, comment = ""}
show_targets_script(pipe)
```

Objects are written as source with `deparse()`, so they must be self-contained: top-level functions and small constants. A closure that depends on its enclosing environment, or a large or non-deparsable object such as a fitted model, belongs in `tt_data()`.

The value is read from the session when you declare it, as `tt_data()` snapshots its object. Re-declaring a name replaces the earlier declaration, so the script holds one assignment per global and every target sees the latest one.

## `tt_single()`

This command adds an operation on a whole target (not iterative/grouped).

```{r summarise}
pipe <- pipe |>
  tt_single(n_samples <- length(sample_names))
```

```{r summarise-script, comment = ""}
show_targets_script(pipe)
```

Mapped lists from `tt_initialise()` and `tt_data_list()` are registered as stem list targets (no `map()` in the script) and marked as units for later `tt_iterate()`. File-tracking targets are stems too.

## `tt_iterate()`

Map a function over every input. Write `name <- expr` as you would a `tar_target()` command (`target_output = "name"` still works).

```{r iterate-read}
pipe <- pipe |>
  tt_iterate(data <- input_list * 2)
```

```{r iterate-read-script, comment = ""}
show_targets_script(pipe)
```

A second iterate maps over the result of the first:

```{r iterate-length}
pipe <- pipe |>
  tt_iterate(n <- length(data))
```

```{r iterate-length-script, comment = ""}
show_targets_script(pipe)
```

With two mapped inputs, `tt_iterate()` uses `map()` by default. `{targets}` errors at make if the lengths differ; pass `pattern = "cross"` for a product of branches. A constant (including a length-1 list) belongs in `tt_data()`, not `tt_data_list()`.

## `tt_evaluate()`

```{r evaluate}
pipe |> tt_evaluate()
```

## `tt_explore()`

Return one stored instance of a target so you can inspect it or pipe it onward. A heading names the target (and which instance, for collections). Mapped targets load a single branch rather than every sample.

```{r tt-explore}
pipe |> tt_explore(data)
```

## `tt_read()`

Read the full stored value of a named target (every branch of a mapped target). Compare with `tt_explore()` when you only need one instance.

```{r tt-read}
pipe |> tt_read(data)
```

## `tt_merge()`

Collect every branch of an iterated target into one object.

```{r merge}
pipe <- pipe |>
  tt_merge(n_total <- sum(unlist(n)))
```

```{r merge-script, comment = ""}
show_targets_script(pipe)
```

## `tt_split()`

Inverse of `tt_merge()`: a stem command that returns a list is marked as mapped units. Later `tt_iterate()` steps that mention it branch over the elements. Unlike `tt_data_list()`, the split runs in the pipeline.

```{r split}
grid_split <- expand.grid(alpha = c(0, 1), lambda = c(0.1, 1))
split_pipe <- tt_initialise() |>
  tt_data(grid_split) |>
  tt_split(settings <- grid_split |> group_split(row_number()))
```

```{r split-script, comment = ""}
show_targets_script(split_pipe)
```

## `tt_report()`

Appends a `tarchetypes::tar_quarto_raw()` factory. Rendering happens later, when you evaluate the pipeline; the grammar only writes the target.

```{r report-file}
writeLines(
  c(
    "---",
    "title: Example report",
    "format: html",
    "params:",
    "  n_total: 0",
    "  n_samples: 0",
    "---",
    "",
    "Samples: `r params$n_samples`. Values: `r params$n_total`."
  ),
  "example-report.qmd"
)
```

```{r report}
pipe <- pipe |>
  tt_report(
    target_output = "report",
    rmd_path = "example-report.qmd",
    params = list(n_total = n_total, n_samples = n_samples)
  )
```

```{r report-script, comment = ""}
show_targets_script(pipe)
```

## Custom functions from a file

`tt_iterate()`, `tt_single()`, `tt_split()`, and `tt_merge()` accept `user_function_source_path`. The path is written as `source(...)` in the targets script so workers can load helpers that are not in a package.

```{r source-path, eval = FALSE}
pipe |>
  tt_iterate(
    transformed <- my_transform(data),
    user_function_source_path = "helpers.R"
  )
```

## Submitting jobs to a remote HPC from your local machine

The controller stays in the R session on your machine. A `command_submit` wrapper copies each job script to Gadi and runs `qsub` there. The worker dials back through an SSH tunnel: a compute node has no route to your machine, and Gadi only lets that tunnel listen on the login node's `127.0.0.1`, so `nc` on the login node accepts the compute node and forwards it into the tunnel. The job runs `nc` again, so the worker keeps dialling `127.0.0.1`, which is the address in the certificate `{crew}` creates. One SSH master connection carries the tunnel, the relay, and `qsub`, so all three land on the same login node.

`storage` and `retrieval` have to be `"main"`. The default `"worker"` fails: the compute node tries to read and write the store, and the store is on your machine. `"main"` sends every input to the worker and every result back, so each object passes through the R session on your machine. tidytargets drops an object once it has been saved, but the session holds whatever is in flight. One large object costs about its size in memory, and several workers finishing together cost that several times over.

Save this file, then run the terminal commands, then run the R code.

**File `remote_qsub.sh`.** Save it on your machine, in the directory where you start R, and run `chmod +x remote_qsub.sh`. `{crew}` calls this file instead of `qsub`. It rewrites the script Gadi rejects, copies it to `gadi.nci.org.au`, and submits it. `sed -i ''` is the macOS form.

```{bash remote-qsub, eval = FALSE}
#!/bin/bash
# remote_qsub.sh
set -euo pipefail
script=$1
remote=YOUR_USER@gadi.nci.org.au
dir=/scratch/YOUR_PROJECT/$USER/crew_scripts
sed -i '' \
  -e '/^#PBS -J 1-1$/d' \
  -e 's/^#PBS -l ppn=/#PBS -l ncpus=/' \
  -e 's/^#PBS -l mem=\([0-9.]*\)gb$/#PBS -l mem=\1GB/' \
  "$script"
ssh -S /tmp/gadi.sock "$remote" "mkdir -p $dir && cat > $dir/$(basename "$script")" < "$script"
ssh -S /tmp/gadi.sock "$remote" "/opt/pbs/default/bin/qsub $dir/$(basename "$script")"
```

**Run in your terminal.** The first command logs in to `gadi.nci.org.au` and opens the tunnel back to your machine. The second runs `nc` on that login node and keeps running: it listens on the login node's own address and forwards each connection into the tunnel. Leave it running until the pipeline finishes. Bash cannot listen on a port. `nc` on Gadi is ncat, and `-k` keeps it accepting connections. `hostname -I` prints the login node's address; the R code below calls it `LOGIN_NODE_IP`.

```{bash gadi-tunnel, eval = FALSE}
ssh -o ControlMaster=yes -o ControlPath=/tmp/gadi.sock -o ControlPersist=2h \
  -fN -R 127.0.0.1:47200:127.0.0.1:47200 YOUR_USER@gadi.nci.org.au
ssh -S /tmp/gadi.sock YOUR_USER@gadi.nci.org.au \
  'nc -k -l $(hostname -I | cut -d" " -f1) 47201 -c "nc 127.0.0.1 47200"'
```

**Run in R.** `host` and `port` are the tunnel on your machine. Everything else here is what Gadi needs to start the worker and send it back through that tunnel. The controller uses `{crew}`'s default of one worker, which is the job `remote_qsub.sh` accepts.

```{r pbs, eval = FALSE}
library(crew.cluster)
library(tidytargets)

computing_resources <- crew_controller_pbs(
  host = "127.0.0.1",
  port = 47200,
  options_cluster = crew_options_pbs(
    command_submit = "./remote_qsub.sh",
    script_lines = c(
      "#PBS -P YOUR_PROJECT",
      "#PBS -q express",
      "#PBS -l storage=scratch/YOUR_PROJECT",
      "source /etc/profile.d/modules.sh",
      "module load intel-compiler-llvm/2025.3.2",
      "module load intel-mkl/2025.0.1",
      "module load R/4.5.0",
      "export R_LIBS_USER=/scratch/YOUR_PROJECT/$USER/Rlib",
      "nc -k -l 127.0.0.1 47200 -c 'nc LOGIN_NODE_IP 47201' &",
      "sleep 2"
    )
  )
)

inputs <- list(sample_a = 1:3, sample_b = 4:6)
inputs |>
  tt_initialise(
    computing_resources = computing_resources,
    packages = "tidytargets",
    storage = "main",
    retrieval = "main"
  ) |>
  tt_iterate(summaries <- summary(input_list)) |>
  tt_evaluate()
```
